_README: Second GR86 build, read 2026-08-12. NOT the July car — same chassis, a
completely different build: AWD swap, semi-slick tires at maximum width,
2,428 lb against 2,900, 290 hp / 303 lb-ft against 350 / 260. It is a
separate fixture rather than an edit of gearing-gr86-2026-07-31.json for
exactly that reason. Two builds, both recorded, is what the old data
Six configurations, final drive the only variable, no driving — every
figure is Performance panel output off a screen photograph, which is
digits and so within the photo protocol.
NOTHING POSITIONAL WAS TAKEN FROM AN IMAGE. The axis maximum is a printed
label. The fit is Boston's own on-screen reading, swept live. The graph in
the photographs is ~250 px wide for 157 mph — one pixel is 0.6 mph — so
judging where a line lands from it would be the 3.73 error exactly.
screen: tuning menu — GEARING tab, with the Performance panel alongside

build.twNote: reported as the maximum width the car allows, front and rear. Recorded as +3 because CLAUDE.md has FH6 widths running stock to +3; confirm the actual step count on the upgrade screen.
build.dtNote: DRIVETRAIN SWAP. The GR86 is RWD stock, so this build carries an AWD conversion — which also confirms drivetrain swaps exist in FH6, the assumption the SAT-DT satellite slot rests on.

held.ratiosNote: Read off this screen and IDENTICAL to both SPREAD[7] and the July build's ratios. Boston's read was that they looked edited; they are not — this is the game's own 7-speed race-box default set, now confirmed on two separate builds of the car. SPREAD[7] stands.

rows.rowNote: The three Miscellaneous readouts said SIMULATING... when this shot was taken, so they are null rather than carried over from the previous row. See protocolNotes.

readings.axisMaxNote: Read cold off the bottom axis before the two candidates were looked at, which is what case G1 asks for.
readings.axisMidLabelNote: The axis also prints a midpoint label at 78, and 157/2 = 78.5, so the axis is linear and evenly divided — the assumption every gear-speed calculation makes, never previously checked.
readings.fitNote: Boston's own reading, swept live on the screen: the final drive at which the top gear's line just reaches the right-hand edge. Deliberately NOT re-judged from the photographs.
readings.axisVsGearingNote: CASE G2, ANSWERED. The axis label stayed 157 across every final drive from 3.50 to 4.60. The axis is not a function of the gearing.
readings.axisVsPartsNote: CASE G3, ANSWERED by Boston's own standing observation: the only thing he has ever seen move that number is changing parts and coming back. So the axis IS a property of the build, not of the car alone — which is the mechanism E2 needed, and it means every axis reading must be filed with the build that produced it. This fixture and the July one are two different builds and are correctly two files.
readings.gearEndpointsNote: Not read. Positional, so it needs the live screen; the derived table below is what they would be checked against.

derived._note: COMPUTED, NOT MEASURED. Kept separate from `readings` so the two can never be confused. k = axisMax * fit * topRatio, then per-gear limiter speed = k/(FD*G).
eraseTheDisagreement: THIS IS THE E2 RESULT, AND IT IS AN ARGUMENT RATHER THAN A DIRECT READ.
July recorded fit 4.575 with the axis as either 157 or 159. Today, on a
build that shares almost nothing with it — AWD instead of RWD, 472 lb
lighter, 60 hp down, different tire compound and width — the fit came
back 4.57 and the axis read 157.
Two builds this different landing on the same fit to 0.1% is what makes
157 the reading that survives. 159 requires the constant to have moved
1.4% and then moved back.
WHAT STILL ARGUES FOR 159, and why this is not closed: the July file's
fifthAtFd373 = 145.4 fits k = 596.5 exactly and misses by 2.0 mph at
k = 588.3. That number is only evidence if it was read off the screen
rather than back-computed from 159 at the time — which is exactly what
the July file already flags and nobody can now establish. Under G3 above
there is also a legitimate escape: the July build was a DIFFERENT build,
so its k is allowed to differ from today's.
The decisive experiment, if a GR86 with enough power to hit a limiter is
ever built: gear it short enough to be rev-limited in a middle gear and
compare the Top Speed readout against k/(FD*G). That is the one case
where the readout and the model must agree exactly.

gearSpeedsAtFit._note: limiter speed per gear at the fit, fd 4.57, k 588.3. 7th = 157 by construction — that IS the fit.

whichGearTheCarActuallyReaches: Measured top speed is ~139.9, and that is what decides whether a ratio
does any work. Compare it against the gear BELOW the top one:
fd 4.57 (the fit): 6th runs out at 135.5, top speed 139.9 — so the car
shifts into 7th and uses it. ALL SEVEN GEARS ENGAGE.
fd 4.00:           6th runs out at 154.8, top speed 139.6 — the car
fd 3.50:           5th runs out at 152.8, top speed 139.2 — the car
This reproduces, on a completely different build, the exact argument the
July sweep used to set vFrac = 1.00 for road: the flat part of the
performance surface is broad, and what breaks the tie is that gearing at
the fit is the only setting where every ratio you paid PI for is used.
theTensionWorthRecording: It is not free, though, and this build makes the cost bigger than July's.
0-100 is best at fd 4.00 (8.867) and the fit costs 0.133 s against it
(9.000). July's equivalent gap was 0.035 s. 0-60 goes the other way and
favours the short end (3.333 at 4.56-4.60 against 3.500 at 3.50).
So on this car the honest statement is: gear at the fit and you use the
whole gearbox and give up ~0.13 s to 100; gear at 4.00 and you take the
0.13 s and carry a dead 7th. vFrac = 1.00 stands, but the app should not

protocolNotes: TWO METHOD FINDINGS FROM THIS SITTING, both worth more than a single row.
1. THE PANEL RE-SIMULATES, AND IT IS NOT NOISE-FREE. It prints
'SIMULATING...' while it recomputes — caught at fd 3.50 with three
readouts unsettled — and Boston reports that leaving a final drive and
returning to the SAME setting moves 0-60 and top speed slightly. So the
figures are a re-run simulation rather than a lookup, and one reading is
a sample, not a fact.
THIS OVERTURNS A CLAIM CLAUDE.md AND BACKLOG.md BOTH STATED: that panel
figures carry no run-to-run variance. Both are corrected. Two rules
follow — discard any reading taken while something still says
SIMULATING, and treat a difference smaller than the repeat spread as no
result.
2. THE SPREAD IS VISIBLE IN THIS VERY SWEEP, which is how it was caught.
139.7: non-monotonic, 0.4 mph, across settings 0.04 apart. Under the old
assumption that had to be a real effect of the gearing. Under the
corrected one it is the readout resampling itself.
WHAT THIS COSTS US, STATED PLAINLY: the vFrac calibration sweep in
CLAUDE.md spans 0.12 s across its whole 0-100 range. If the repeat
spread turns out to be a meaningful fraction of that, part of the sweep
that vFrac was fitted to is noise. Establishing the spread — read one
setting five times, leaving and returning between reads — is now the
highest-value two minutes available, because it sets the threshold every
future panel measurement is judged against, retrospectively included.
notes: Two free controls came out of the sweep. LATERAL G IS COMPLETELY INSENSITIVE TO GEARING — 1.26 at 60 and 1.42 at 120 on all six rows — which is what makes it usable as a grip instrument later (case S5) without holding the final drive. BRAKING IS NOT: 60-0 moved 67.1 -> 68.0 ft and 100-0 moved 151.8 -> 152.8 between fd 4.56 and fd 3.50, presumably engine braking, so the brake work in case S4 must hold the final drive fixed or it will be measuring gearing. Mechanical Balance 0.51 and Aero Balance 0.45 held across every row, confirming they do not respond to gearing, but both remain unusable in the balance solve until the ARB and wing slider values that produced them are read.
